section_1.title: Introduction: The Chaos in the Coffee Cup
section_1.content: Define turbulence as a multi-scale energy cascade. Introduce the Reynolds number (Re) as the dimensionless ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces. Establish the prerequisite: Understanding fluid motion via the Navier-Stokes equations.
section_1.example: Visualize a character stirring cream into coffee. Small swirls appear within larger swirls, illustrating the cascade from large-scale energy injection to small-scale dissipation.

section_2.title: Kolmogorov’s Hypothesis: The Universal Constant
section_2.content: Explain the K41 theory. Focus on the 'Universal Constant' (Kolmogorov constant, C ≈ 1.5). Introduce the concept of the inertial subrange where the energy spectrum follows a power-law distribution.
section_2.example: Display a log-log plot animation showing the energy spectrum decay line with a slope of -5/3, demonstrating the mathematical 'fingerprint' of turbulence.

section_3.title: The Dissipation Scale: Where Chaos Ends
section_3.content: Define the Kolmogorov length scale (η). Discuss how kinetic energy is finally converted into heat at this microscopic scale. Mathematical relationship: η = (ν³/ε)^(1/4).
section_3.example: An animation of a tiny 'micro-robot' diving into the smallest eddies, showing how flow velocity gradient leads to thermal agitation (friction) at the η scale.

section_4.title: The Mathematical Structure: The Energy Cascade
section_4.content: Synthesize the structure: Energy injection (large scales) → Inertial range (transfer, constant flux) → Dissipation (small scales). Emphasize the mathematical invariance of the energy transfer rate (ε).
section_4.example: A graphical flow-chart of 'Energy Buckets' passing fluid kinetic energy from giant vortex buckets down to the tiny dissipation bucket, maintaining a steady, scale-invariant flow.

section_5.title: Summary and Conclusion
section_5.content: Review the importance of these constants in modern engineering (e.g., aerodynamics, weather modeling). Reiterate that turbulence is not random, but follows strict mathematical self-similarity.
section_5.example: A side-by-side comparison: A falcon diving (large scale) and the turbulent wake generated at its wingtips (small scale), showing the same universal mathematical structure at play.
